title: Pediatric Orthopaedic Surgery Fellowship

prerequisites.level: Advanced post-residency self-study for licensed physicians/orthopaedic trainees; not introductory medical school material.
prerequisites.required: Prior orthopaedic surgery residency-level anatomy, biomechanics, trauma, imaging, evidence appraisal, and professional communication. ACGME describes fellowship as advanced education beyond core residency.
prerequisites.limits: No supervised patients, procedural lab, clinical exposure, case log, feedback by credentialed faculty, or competency sign-off is provided.

objectives: Synthesize age- and growth-aware pediatric musculoskeletal differentials and identify urgent red flags.
Interpret clinical/imaging descriptions judiciously and state uncertainty and limitations.
Explain major ACGME pediatric orthopaedic domains: trauma, hip, spine, neuromuscular, deformity, foot/ankle, infection/tumor, upper limb, rehabilitation and scholarship.
Critically appraise public guideline/research evidence and communicate family-centered, multidisciplinary reasoning.
Differentiate independent study from accredited fellowship, supervised procedures, licensure and board certification.

units.title: Foundations: growth, examination, imaging and pediatric safety
objectives: Relate growth plates and skeletal maturity to age-specific anatomy and fracture interpretation.
Structure history and exam around developmental stage, gait, neurovascular status and family context.
Choose imaging/tests judiciously and identify when urgent escalation is needed.
topics: Physeal biology; normal variants; growth and remodeling; pediatric MSK exam; radiograph quality; safeguarding and documentation.
boardDomains: ACGME competency: judicious diagnostic testing, data interpretation, imaging, professionalism, communication.
units.casePractice: Fictional vignette: build a structured history/examination and safe escalation note for a child with an unexplained limp; do not infer abuse from one finding.
units.assessment: Submit one-page age-aware examination/imaging plan; score /4 each for developmental context, differential, test justification, safety/communication (16 points).

units.title: Acute fractures, physeal injury and pediatric trauma
objectives: Classify common pediatric fracture patterns and identify urgent neurovascular/compartment concerns.
Explain how age, fracture stability, remodeling potential and physeal involvement shape a differential of management options.
Present trauma decisions and follow-up needs without treating an algorithm as a procedure credential.
topics: Supracondylar, forearm, distal radius, femur and physeal injuries; polytrauma; non-accidental injury differential; complications and growth arrest.
boardDomains: ACGME essential conditions: supracondylar fracture, upper/lower-limb trauma, femoral shaft fracture; trauma acute/reconstructive.
units.casePractice: Fictional case: interpret a text-only description of a displaced elbow fracture plus pulse/perfusion findings and outline immediate assessment, team escalation and observation priorities.
units.assessment: Case brief /20: red-flag triage 5, age/growth-aware reasoning 5, complication surveillance 5, communication/family explanation 5.

units.title: Developmental hip: DDH and infant hip decision frameworks
objectives: Describe age/development-dependent DDH assessment principles and the purpose/limits of imaging.
Compare observation, bracing and operative decision questions at a conceptual level using guideline scope.
Plan surveillance questions and recognize reduction/vascular/growth complications as supervised-care concerns.
topics: Hip development; screening/diagnostic uncertainty; pre-walking DDH; imaging; treatment options and complications; adolescent residual dysplasia overview.
boardDomains: ACGME DDH before walking age and hip reconstruction; imaging, natural history and indications.
units.casePractice: Fictional consult: state which information is missing before interpreting an infant hip study; distinguish screening result, diagnosis and treatment decision.
units.assessment: Guideline appraisal /16: question/population 4, recommendation and evidence scope 4, uncertainty/harms 4, follow-up/family communication 4.

units.title: Adolescent hip: SCFE, Perthes and hip preservation differentials
objectives: Recognize why suspected SCFE is an urgent clinical problem and list safe next steps without delaying escalation.
Differentiate age-pattern, symptoms and imaging questions for SCFE and Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.
Frame hip preservation decisions as individualized and supervised.
topics: SCFE stability and complications; Perthes natural history; adolescent dysplasia and impingement differential; hip exam and imaging.
boardDomains: ACGME SCFE; hip conditions; appropriate diagnostic tests and complication management.
units.casePractice: Fictional case comparison: write a differential for a teenager with referred knee pain and restricted hip rotation; identify urgent alternatives.
units.assessment: Oral-viva outline /20: differential 5, red flags 5, imaging reasoning 5, uncertainty/communication 5.

units.title: Spine deformity and spinal safety
objectives: Distinguish broad scoliosis categories and explain growth/maturity relevance.
Interpret a radiographic description with attention to curve measurement reliability and secondary causes.
Identify neurologic/systemic red flags and multidisciplinary planning needs.
topics: Adolescent idiopathic, congenital, neuromuscular scoliosis; sagittal balance; screening limits; bracing/surgical decision domains; high-risk spine review.
boardDomains: ACGME idiopathic scoliosis, spine deformity and neuromuscular conditions; perioperative care.
units.casePractice: Fictional imaging report: explain what curve magnitude and skeletal maturity do and do not answer; make a follow-up question list.
units.assessment: Reasoning rubric /16: classification 4, maturity/context 4, red flags 4, shared decision/follow-up 4.

units.title: Neuromuscular conditions, cerebral palsy and gait
objectives: Relate tone, motor function, hip surveillance and functional goals in a multidisciplinary assessment.
Compare musculoskeletal manifestations across cerebral palsy and selected neuromuscular/genetic disorders.
Distinguish impairment correction from patient-centered functional outcomes.
topics: CP, gait, muscular dystrophy, Down syndrome, OI; hip displacement; contracture; orthoses, therapy, perioperative coordination.
boardDomains: ACGME cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy, Down syndrome, OI; allied health; non-operative/operative continuity.
units.casePractice: Fictional multidisciplinary conference: formulate goals and questions for family, PT/OT and neurology; avoid one-size-fits-all surgical claims.
units.assessment: Conference brief /20: functional goal 5, multidisciplinary roles 5, risk/benefit uncertainty 5, family communication 5.

units.title: Foot and ankle: clubfoot, deformity and growth
objectives: Outline the principles and serial decision checkpoints of Ponseti management without presenting this as procedural instruction.
Classify common foot deformity patterns and distinguish flexible from rigid presentations.
Plan relapse surveillance and family-centered adherence discussion.
topics: Idiopathic/atypical clubfoot; casting principles; relapse; flatfoot, cavus, vertical talus; ankle/foot trauma; orthoses.
boardDomains: ACGME clubfoot, other foot/ankle deformity, rehabilitation and orthotics.
units.casePractice: Fictional longitudinal vignette: describe what change in foot findings would prompt reassessment and specialist review.
units.assessment: Rubric /16: deformity description 4, management-stage logic 4, relapse/safety 4, family-centered communication 4.

units.title: Limb alignment, discrepancy and guided growth
objectives: Describe a reproducible framework for measuring alignment and limb-length discrepancy.
Explain growth remaining as a key uncertainty in timing and treatment options.
Compare observation, orthoses, guided growth and reconstruction as conceptual choices requiring specialist planning.
topics: Coronal/sagittal/rotational alignment; Blount disease; hemiepiphysiodesis; lengthening; growth prediction limits; congenital limb deficiency.
boardDomains: ACGME lower/upper-limb deformity, deranged growth and limb discrepancy; normal growth physiology.
units.casePractice: Fictional planning task: identify measurements and maturity data needed before comparing options for progressive angular deformity.
units.assessment: Planning rubric /20: measurements 5, growth uncertainty 5, alternatives/risks 5, follow-up and consent 5.

units.title: Tumors, infection and inflammatory/metabolic mimics
objectives: Construct a time-sensitive differential for bone pain, fever or lesion found on imaging.
Separate infection, benign lesions, malignancy and inflammatory/metabolic conditions using appropriate evidence and consultation.
Explain why biopsy/antibiotic/treatment sequencing requires a coordinated specialist team.
topics: Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis; septic arthritis overlap; bone lesions and tumor referral; JIA/CRMO; OI/metabolic disease; labs/imaging limitations.
boardDomains: ACGME infection, tumors, metabolic/genetic conditions; diagnostics, complications and research appraisal.
units.casePractice: Fictional case: child with fever and focal bone pain; list differential, urgent tests/consults and what data could change the assessment.
units.assessment: Evidence brief /20: differential 5, test selection 5, urgent coordination 5, uncertainty/source use 5.

units.title: Upper extremity, hand and sports-related pediatric conditions
objectives: Apply skeletal immaturity to upper-limb trauma and overuse reasoning.
Recognize common pediatric elbow, shoulder, hand and wrist patterns and important complications.
Discuss return-to-activity decisions as individualized shared planning.
topics: Elbow ossification and fractures; medial epicondyle; forearm/wrist; hand trauma; throwing athlete; physeal overuse; instability and knee sport injuries.
boardDomains: ACGME upper-limb trauma, hand disorders, athletic injuries, sports exposure.
units.casePractice: Fictional athlete case: distinguish an injury description from a definitive return-to-sport decision; propose relevant data and stakeholders.
units.assessment: Rubric /16: maturation pattern 4, differential 4, complications 4, shared decision 4.

units.title: Perioperative care, complications, rehabilitation and continuity
objectives: Recognize common categories of postoperative complications and escalation triggers.
Integrate pain/function, wound, neurovascular and rehabilitation follow-up in a continuity plan.
Discuss consent, assent, accessibility, safety and family communication.
topics: Perioperative planning; cast/implant issues; infection; neurovascular compromise; growth disturbance; rehabilitation; transitions and patient safety.
boardDomains: ACGME postoperative continuity, recovery/rehab, complications, communication, systems-based practice.
units.casePractice: Fictional handover exercise: create a contingency-aware follow-up summary from a mock discharge vignette.
units.assessment: Handover rubric /20: problem list 5, red flags 5, follow-up contingencies 5, plain-language family communication 5.

units.title: Scholarship, quality improvement and board-cognitive integration
objectives: Critically appraise a clinical study and identify design, bias and applicability limits.
Build a measurable QI question and define process/outcome/balancing measures.
Synthesize differential, evidence, risks and communication under timed oral/written conditions.
topics: Study design; evidence hierarchy; QI; ethics/IRB; journal club; case presentation; morbidity/mortality; lifelong learning.
boardDomains: ACGME research methods, practice-based learning, weekly teaching, monthly M&M and journal club; no separate pediatric-orthopaedic ABOS board exam.
units.casePractice: Fictional QI: propose a measure to improve completeness of neurovascular documentation without assuming local baseline data.
units.assessment: Capstone /24: clinical synthesis 6, evidence appraisal 6, QI design 6, explicit scope/safety caveats 6.

assignment.title: Longitudinal fictional case conference and evidence appraisal
assignment.brief: Choose one fictional text-only scenario from Units 2–11. Submit a 1,200–1,500 word structured problem representation, prioritized differential, age/growth-aware data needs, guideline/evidence appraisal, complications/safety discussion, multidisciplinary/family communication plan, and one explicit “what cannot be inferred” paragraph. Add a 1-page QI proposal with process, outcome and balancing measures. Do not use real patient records or unlicensed images.

rubric.criterion: Privacy, image permissions and limits of self-study

assignment.passInterpretation: For self-assessment only; not validated, credentialing, board-predictive or clinical competence assessment.

assessment.format: Ten original multiple-choice items with rationales; unit-based fictional case briefs; capstone rubric.
assessment.rubric: Practice questions are educational original content, not official exam items. Review wrong answers against linked primary sources. No passing threshold predicts certification or patient-care competence.
assessment.blueprintNote: Curriculum maps to 2026 ACGME program requirement domains as educational domains. ABOS primary certification is distinct; no separate pediatric orthopaedic ABOS examination. It is not represented as the official ABOS/OITE exam blueprint.

studyHours.plan: Illustrative 12-week self-study plan: 4 hours/week reading and notes, 2 hours/week case/application, 1 hour/week retrieval practice = 84 learner-hours total. Excludes any unverified or planned video time; adapt to learner needs. Not clinical training hours.

topicGaps: Verified free public recordings with directly observed duration total 1.0789 hours (3,884 seconds); the 36-hour target remains short by 34.9211 hours. Authored scripts and planned clip target minutes are not rendered or verified media and do not reduce this gap.

Free item-level lecture coverage remains narrow. The public Stanford series includes 14 playlist entries, with 3 unavailable items hidden; the DDH/SCFE and clubfoot entries inspected during this pass explicitly returned “Video unavailable” and were excluded. Other public playlist listings without item-level playback/runtime evidence were not counted.

Substantive source-backed teaching remains insufficient for specialist-depth scoliosis/congenital spine, CP and neuromuscular gait, limb-growth prediction/guided growth, clubfoot technique, pediatric bone tumors, upper-extremity/hand conditions, perioperative complications/rehabilitation, and QI/research methods. Public study pages and requirements documents are not a complete lecture curriculum.

AAOS pediatric DDH recommendations are limited to typically developing infants younger than six months; PIDS/IDSA AHO guidance is limited to otherwise healthy children 1 month to under 18 in North America and excludes neonates and several infection contexts. The curriculum preserves these limits.

The legacy 180-minute originalClipPlan targets are planning metadata only. They are not completed scripts, rendered recordings, observed runtime, or verified hours. Four full original scripts address selected teaching gaps; source feasibility for generating 34.9211 hours of non-padding original recordings is not established.

boardNames: American Board of Orthopaedic Surgery (ABOS) — primary orthopaedic surgery certification; no separate ABOS Pediatric Orthopaedic Surgery subspecialty certificate/examination is listed as of 2026-10-07
medical.boardStatus: ABOS lists two subspecialty certificates (Surgery of the Hand and Orthopaedic Sports Medicine), not pediatric orthopaedics. Pediatric orthopaedic surgery is an ACGME-accredited clinical fellowship specialty, not a separate ABOS subspecialty examination. POSNA directory listing/accreditation does not confer board certification. Verify individual primary ABOS eligibility with ABOS; this curriculum cannot confer eligibility.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: The Boston Children’s programme page says it is open to applicants who completed ACGME/ACGME-I-accredited (or Canadian equivalent) orthopaedic surgery residency and are eligible for Massachusetts licensure. ACGME 2026 requirements contain a narrow exceptionally qualified international graduate exception subject to program/GMEC review and ECFMG certification, and warn training may not lead to ABMS/AOA certification. This is not an eligibility determination. No separate ABOS pediatric orthopaedic examination/certificate is listed. Check current programme/board rules.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 12-year-old with progressive limp and referred knee pain has limited hip internal rotation. What is the safest reasoning priority?

options.text: Assume knee pathology because pain is at the knee
Consider a hip source including SCFE and arrange urgent appropriate evaluation
Begin return-to-sport testing before imaging
Diagnose Perthes from age alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hip disease can present as knee pain; suspected SCFE warrants prompt specialist assessment. Age and one sign do not establish diagnosis.
practiceQuestions.domain: ACGME SCFE domain; POSNA Study Guide SCFE

practiceQuestions.stem: An infant’s ultrasound is reported as borderline. Which statement best distinguishes evidence from decision?

options.text: One borderline result establishes need for surgery
Interpretation depends on age, exam, imaging quality, and guideline context; confirm appropriate follow-up
All infants need CT
No follow-up is needed if asymptomatic

practiceQuestions.rationale: Screening/diagnostic results need age- and context-aware interpretation; guidelines inform but do not replace individualized assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with a forearm fracture has increasing pain and tense swelling. What is the key cognitive response?

options.text: Reassure because pediatric bones remodel
Treat as a possible urgent complication and reassess neurovascular/compartment status promptly
Wait for routine clinic
Assume normal cast discomfort without examination

practiceQuestions.rationale: Worsening disproportionate pain and tense swelling can indicate a limb-threatening complication requiring urgent clinical assessment. This item is a safety concept, not protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about an open educational video is enough to count its hours in this course?

options.text: Search result title says lecture
Runtime is estimated from topic
Public playback and canonical ID/runtime are directly verified with evidence
A playlist’s advertised total is assumed

practiceQuestions.rationale: Only observed duration and publicly accessible playback on a unique source ID can be counted; this candidate set has zero verified hours.
practiceQuestions.domain: Contract methodology; source metadata needs direct verification

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has fever and focal bone pain. Which approach is best?

options.text: Name osteomyelitis without considering alternatives
Build a differential and select investigations/consults using current pediatric infection guidance and clinical urgency
Delay assessment until symptoms resolve
Treat all bone pain with surgery

practiceQuestions.rationale: Infection is one important possibility, but differential diagnosis, appropriate investigations, and urgent clinical assessment are required.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is an accurate summary of this fellowship’s separate board status?

options.text: ABOS offers a Pediatric Orthopaedic Surgery subspecialty exam
ABOS lists Hand and Orthopaedic Sports Medicine subspecialty certificates, not pediatric orthopaedics
POSNA directory listing confers a board certificate
Completing this self-study course creates board eligibility

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABOS page lists two subspecialty certificates; pediatric orthopaedics is a clinical fellowship specialty without a separate ABOS certificate/exam listed. Primary orthopaedic board certification is distinct.

practiceQuestions.stem: Why does skeletal maturity matter in deformity planning?

options.text: It precisely predicts every future millimeter of growth
Remaining growth affects timing and options, but prediction is uncertain and patient-specific
It is irrelevant to guided growth
It determines diagnosis by itself

practiceQuestions.rationale: Growth remaining is central to timing decisions but prediction is imperfect; use multiple clinical/radiographic inputs and specialist judgment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A published radiograph is visible on a free site. What permission can the course assume?

options.text: Free viewing means public domain
Permission to rehost is implied
No reuse right; check individual license, attribution, consent/de-identification and purpose
The image may be downloaded for any teaching use

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free access is not permission to copy or redistribute clinical images; rights and privacy must be checked case-by-case.

practiceQuestions.stem: During a scoliosis case discussion, which conclusion is appropriately limited?

options.text: One curve measurement alone determines treatment
Combine curve description, skeletal maturity, symptoms, cause and patient goals; use specialist standards
All curves progress identically
Patient education webpage is an operative guideline

practiceQuestions.rationale: Curve measurement is only one element; classification, maturity, etiology, context, evidence, and shared decisions matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: A student proposes teaching a Ponseti casting technique from a video. What caveat is essential?

options.text: Video viewing demonstrates procedural competence
A conceptual overview can support knowledge, but technique requires supervised clinical training and assessment
No follow-up is required
Any cast schedule applies to all feet

practiceQuestions.rationale: Video learning cannot establish procedural competence; casting and management require appropriate supervised training.
practiceQuestions.domain: ACGME procedure requirements; Ponseti International overview

title: Pediatric Orthopaedics Fellowship
prerequisites: Physician learners with prior orthopaedic surgery residency-level foundation; fellowship entry requirements are governed by programme and applicable accreditation rules, not this course.
Foundational anatomy, growth and development, fracture principles, imaging interpretation, evidence appraisal, and pediatric communication.
Learners without clinical credentials may use materials only for general education; no patient care or procedural use.
objectives: Synthesize age-specific pediatric orthopaedic history, examination and imaging.
Interpret pediatric musculoskeletal growth, fracture and deformity problems using published evidence and board-domain frameworks.
Identify urgent threats, uncertainty, scope limitations and appropriate escalation in fictional cases.
Evaluate DDH, adolescent hip, trauma, spine, neuromuscular, sports, foot/ankle, infection and bone-lesion topics.
Communicate family-centered, ethical and team-based reasoning.
Distinguish institutional fellowship training, ACGME accreditation, ABOS primary certification and practice-profiled MOC examination.

units.title: Pediatric growth, development and fellowship reasoning

Distinguish normal developmental variation from disease while stating uncertainty.

age-linked developmental variation; growth context and limits of remodeling; separating observations from hypotheses
boardDomains: General (growth and development, including physis and anatomy; 3%)
casePractice: case: age-tagged films from POSNA topic guide; annotate physis, do not copy

units.title: Pediatric musculoskeletal examination and imaging selection
objectives: Build a focused age-appropriate history and exam for pain, deformity, gait or injury.

limp as symptom; age-anchored differential; red-flag review; communicating what normal imaging does and does not establish
boardDomains: General (growth and development, including physis and anatomy; 3%)
casePractice: fictional limping-child differential; use only openly viewable examples in POSNA guide
units.assessment: Write imaging rationale for three scenarios; rubric: question-fit 40%, interpretation limits 30%, radiation/communication 30%.

units.title: DDH: screening, evaluation and management principles
objectives: Apply age-dependent examination and imaging principles to DDH.
Use the AAOS guideline within its defined population and identify when its scope does not apply.
topics: risk factors; Barlow/Ortolani context; ultrasound vs radiograph; referral; nonoperative management; guideline scope <6 months
source population, evidence strength and date; infant DDH guidance must not be generalized to older children or complex patients
casePractice: AAOS CPG PDF and POSNA DDH topic; do not download patient films
units.assessment: Fictional infant case, evidence table and scope critique; rubric: correct population 25%, evidence 35%, reasoning 25%, safety 15%.

units.title: Adolescent hip: SCFE, Perthes and hip pain differential
objectives: Recognize urgent features and imaging logic for SCFE and differentiate common pediatric hip presentations.
Interpret classifications as decision aids, not substitutes for judgment.
topics: SCFE stability/urgency; Perthes evolution and prognosis; referred knee pain; transient synovitis/septic arthritis differential
Perthes disease update; referred knee pain; limping-child age-based differential; septic-arthritis warning features and urgent escalation
casePractice: SCFE recording; POSNA SCFE and Perthes topics; fictional case
units.assessment: Compare-and-contrast matrix plus emergency escalation rationale; rubric: urgency 35%, differential 25%, imaging 20%, caveats 20%.

units.title: Pediatric fracture principles and common upper-extremity injuries
objectives: Account for physis, remodeling, neurovascular status and compartment risk in pediatric fractures.
Explain why alignment/management thresholds depend on age, fracture and evidence.
topics: supracondylar fractures; elbow and forearm; physeal injury; neurovascular assessment; reduction/casting concepts; complications
fracture description before classification; occult elbow fracture clues; structured motor, sensory and perfusion documentation
casePractice: POSNA fracture study guide, selected topics; no image rehosting
units.assessment: Structured fictional fracture reading; rubric: safety 30%, anatomy 25%, interpretation 25%, management rationale 20%.

units.title: Lower-extremity trauma and acute limb threats
objectives: Prioritize limb-threatening findings and systematic evaluation of lower-extremity injury.
Discuss fracture patterns without converting a vignette into a treatment order.
topics: femur/tibia/ankle; open injury principles; compartment syndrome; polytrauma; physeal injury; follow-up risk
limp and functional change as possible indicators of urgent lower-extremity pathology; escalation is distinct from a treatment order

physeal-risk concepts and evidence update questions for pediatric knee claims

casePractice: Stanford pediatric knee grand rounds recording; POSNA knee topics

safe differential across infection/inflammatory disease, bone lesions and metabolic conditions; source/date limits and time-sensitive escalation

objectives: Use outcomes and evidence quality to compare options without claiming certainty.
Apply consent, safeguarding, equity, teamwork and transitions principles to pediatric orthopaedic scenarios.

functional outcomes and global/context-sensitive service delivery; distinguish educational lectures from local protocols and credentialing

casePractice: ACGME requirements; ABOS blueprint; POSNA review guide

assignment.title: Cumulative pediatric orthopaedics evidence portfolio
deliverables: Twelve unit concept/checkpoint submissions (one per unit).
Three fictional case analyses: infant hip, acute pediatric fracture, and progressive deformity.
One source critique mapping a topic to the ABOS published pediatric MOC blueprint and explaining why that blueprint is not initial board certification.
A capstone concise oral-style synthesis with differential, evidence, safety, uncertainty and family communication.

rubric.evidenceAccuracy: 25%: primary/authoritative sources, dates and guideline scope accurately represented.
rubric.clinicalReasoning: 25%: age-aware problem representation, differential, imaging question and uncertainty.
rubric.safetyEthics: 25%: urgent threats, escalation, no unsupervised treatment advice; correct rights handling.
rubric.communication: 15%: clear family/team-facing explanation and structured handoff.

practiceQuestions.stem: In an infant younger than six months, which resource most directly supplies evidence-based guidance for DDH detection and nonoperative management?

options.text: AAOS 2022 DDH CPG
ABOS general recertification blueprint
ACGME case log form
POSNA match directory

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAOS guideline is specifically scoped to typically developing children under six months and detection/nonoperative management. It does not govern all DDH scenarios or replace specialist judgment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public programme page says “Non-Standard” accrediting body and 1 year duration. What is the safest interpretation?

options.text: Treat it as ACGME-accredited because all fellowships are
Record the institutional listing as non-standard and verify separately against ACGME
Assume it is research-only
Infer ABOS certification eligibility

practiceQuestions.rationale: The Hopkins fellowship directory explicitly lists “Non-Standard”; do not silently relabel it ACGME-accredited or infer board eligibility. Current official programme wording must be reported.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes pediatric orthopaedics and ABOS subspecialty certification?

options.text: ABOS offers a pediatric orthopaedics subspecialty certificate
Pediatric orthopaedics is not one of ABOS’s two subspecialty certificates, though a pediatric practice-profiled MOC exam exists
The fellowship itself guarantees a separate board
No ABOS pediatric assessment exists

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABOS lists only Hand and Orthopaedic Sports Medicine subspecialty certificates. It separately lists pediatric orthopaedic surgery among practice-profiled continuing-certification examinations, distinct from initial certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the appropriate use of an online pediatric case/image resource in this independent course?

options.text: Copy and republish images because cases are educational
Link to the resource, check its terms, and do not copy images or patient records
Assume de-identified means public domain
Create synthetic diagnostic images and label them real

practiceQuestions.rationale: Public viewing is not a rehosting license. Link to authentic cases, verify rights, and do not reproduce images or patient records without explicit permission.

practiceQuestions.stem: A school-age child has atraumatic limp and hip stiffness. What is the reasoning priority before selecting a diagnosis?

options.text: Assess age, systemic appearance, exam and urgent differential, then choose imaging
Diagnose Perthes from knee pain alone
Order MRI for every child
Use one classification as diagnosis

practiceQuestions.rationale: Structured age-appropriate assessment and red-flag differential precede diagnosis; hip disease may refer pain to the knee but that is not diagnostic.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the most defensible way to describe an ABOS pediatric practice-profiled test?

options.text: A separate initial board that all fellows must pass
A continuing-certification exam option for ABOS diplomates, not proof of fellowship board certification
An ACGME accreditation survey
A universal licensing examination

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABOS presents these as practice-profiled examinations under Continuing Certification. They are not a universal initial board or licensure exam.

practiceQuestions.stem: The AAOS DDH CPG’s stated target population is:

options.text: All ages and all DDH interventions
Typically developing children under six months, detection and nonoperative management
Adolescents undergoing pelvic osteotomy
Only children after failed surgery

practiceQuestions.rationale: The published guideline states its scope: detection and nonoperative management of hip instability/dysplasia in typically developing children younger than six months.

It can be counted twice if embedded on two pages
It is official exam content

practiceQuestions.rationale: An institution linking to an unlisted recording is evidence of a viewing pathway, not a grant of reproduction rights or permanent availability.

title: Pediatric Pain Medicine Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (one ACGME-accredited combined pediatric/adult track and a separate non-ACGME pediatric pain training option documented by the same institution)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Physician-level introductory self-study; intended for residents/fellows and practicing clinicians who already possess foundational medical training.
Prior learning: developmental physiology, general pharmacology, pediatric assessment, evidence-based medicine and patient safety.
Not suitable as a substitute for medical school, residency, supervised fellowship, institutional credentialing or hands-on competency assessment.
Learners without clinical training may use public readings for general education but must not apply them to diagnose or treat patients.
objectives: Synthesize developmentally appropriate pain science, assessment and communication.
Select and interpret pain measures with attention to self-report, behavioral tools, function and reassessment.
Reason across pediatric acute/procedural, chronic primary/secondary, cancer, neuropathic, visceral and complex pain topics.
Explain source-backed multimodal, rehabilitation, psychological and pharmacological principles with current scope and safety qualifiers.
Interpret published ACGME requirements and board pathways without conflating program admission, accredited training, board eligibility or certification.
Use evidence and board-blueprint domains for study organization, without representing the course as validated board preparation.
Recognize self-study limits for diagnosis, prescribing, procedural performance and supervised care.

topicGaps: 33.7336 hours remain below the 36-hour target floor after counting six unique publicly listed recordings totaling 8159 seconds (2.2664 hours). The EMSC duration pages report five runtimes at whole-minute precision; only the 8:59 SKIP video has a second-level runtime. No scripted or planned minutes are included.

Recorded-video coverage is still sparse: six additions focus on emergency pain, sickle-cell acute/chronic pain, psychological strategies, an intranasal demonstration, comfort positioning, and needle fear. Insufficient verified lecture coverage remains for pediatric pain neuroscience/development, validated assessment across neonatal and disability contexts, perioperative/regional anesthesia, medication pharmacology/adjuvant safety, cancer and palliative pain, headache/orofacial, visceral/abdominal, neuropathic and musculoskeletal syndromes, CRPS evaluation, research methods and interventional/procedural pain.

The 43-minute OPENPediatrics forum provides cognitive coverage of pediatric chronic and procedural pain psychology but is not a substitute for full rehabilitation training; the 46-minute sickle-cell talk and 28-minute ED overview are historical expert education, not current protocols. Apply date- and setting-specific guidelines and current institutional pathways.

The original UCSF pediatric pain lecture remains a useful public candidate but exact full runtime was not verified, so it remains in unknownDurationItems and is not counted. ChildKind archive recordings have relevant content but no individual duration ledger. OPENPediatrics advertises approximately three hours for an entire course without a per-recording measured ledger. Mary Bridge requires paid registration; Nemours source expiry remains unresolved.

The free public EMSC/HRSA-supported resource index gives exact minute-level duration labels and embeds the counted watch pages. Whole-minute entries are conservatively represented as the stated number of minutes in seconds, with 60-second precision recorded; EMSC does not expose second-level player runtimes. End-to-end playback was not tested using a stateful browser.

Topic gaps remain in pediatric-specialty depth; the ABA Pain Medicine blueprint is an adult/interdisciplinary parent-specialty blueprint, not a pediatric board exam or proof of pediatric readiness. No separate pediatric pain board examination was identified in the official materials already cited.

Five full authored teaching episodes in the separate authored JSON are scripts only: none is recorded, rendered, uploaded, or included in verifiedExternalHours. Their teaching cannot close the media-hour gap.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship (one ACGME-accredited combined pediatric/adult track and a separate non-ACGME pediatric pain training option documented by the same institution)
boardNames: American Board of Anesthesiology (ABA) Pain Medicine subspecialty certification/exam
American Board of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (ABPMR) Pain Medicine subspecialty certification
American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN) Pain Medicine subspecialty certification
medical.boardStatus: Pain Medicine is an interdisciplinary subspecialty with shared examination standards. ABA offers the exam and publishes a 200-item blueprint with General (50%) and Clinical States (50%) domains. ABPMR and ABPN credential eligible diplomates through their own board pathways; ABA administers/develops the shared examination. No separate Pediatric Pain Medicine board exam or pediatric-only board certification was identified in the official sources checked. The BCH ACGME fellowship is an ACGME Pain Medicine fellowship with pediatric focus and adult rotations, not a distinct pediatric board. BCH also describes a separate non-ACGME 3–12 month educational option. Pediatricians are not thereby made pain-medicine board eligible: ABPN requirements specify neurology/child neurology/psychiatry diplomates; ABPMR requires ABPMR diplomate status; ABA requirements must be verified directly for the candidate’s primary board. ACGME eligibility is not equivalent to board eligibility.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course confers no eligibility. Candidate must independently verify current primary-board certification, approved prior residency, program-specific eligibility and examination requirements with the relevant board and fellowship director before applying. Eligibility and board rules checked 2026-10-07; requirements may change.

officialProgrammes.institution: Boston Children’s Hospital (Harvard Medical School teaching hospital)
officialProgrammes.name: Pediatric Pain Medicine Fellowship — ACGME-accredited Combined Pediatric and Adult Pain Medicine Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official BCH GME page says 12 months, ACGME accredited and ABA approved; six months pediatric BCH rotations (acute pain, regional anesthesia, chronic/headache clinics, acupuncture, rehabilitation center, selected pediatric subspecialty rotations) and six months at BIDMC/BWH adult pain medicine centers. Page describes Monday–Thursday departmental didactics, recorded OpenPediatrics lectures and case/journal-club activities. Publicly stated program brochure-style curriculum is informative but not an exhaustive didactic syllabus, annual schedule or procedure log.

officialProgrammes.name: Pediatric Pain Medicine Fellowship — non-ACGME accredited training option (separate track)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Same GME page separately identifies a non-ACGME, unfunded, tailored 3–12 month option combining clinical, research and administrative training, often for physicians not eligible for ABA pain board certification or not pursuing board eligibility. It explicitly says procedural proficiency is not a goal for the non-ACGME fellow. Not interchangeable with the 12-month accredited combined fellowship and not a separate board credential.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The assigned official packet names the BCH GME Pediatric Pain Medicine Fellowship; its official page explicitly documents the ACGME combined adult/pediatric option and a separate non-ACGME track. No additional Harvard-affiliated or Johns Hopkins pediatric pain physician fellowship variant was established for this assigned item. This course does not claim a complete current external programme-directory census; ACGME public search is dynamic.
sourceCaveats: Current official BCH page accessed; its detailed public curriculum describes rotations and teaching but is not a complete annual didactic log. ACGME accreditation statement is program self-description; no independent current accreditation-directory record was validated here.

Current ACGME 2025 requirements and current board pages were checked 2026-10-07; changing eligibility/exam dates should be rechecked with each board. The assignment source links are public, but training and certification pathways are not interchangeable.

No separate pediatric pain board examination or pediatric pain-only specialty certificate was located in ABA, ABPMR or ABPN official materials. This is a bounded finding from these primary sources, not proof no additional credential exists anywhere.
Video hours are deliberately zero because runtime/free complete view could not be established. Nothing planned is represented as a ready video.

No human clinical review performed. This independent learning curriculum has no Harvard, Johns Hopkins, Boston Children’s or board affiliation; grants no accredited training, licensure, board eligibility, procedure competence, certification or guarantee of passing. It cannot replace medical education or supervised patient care.

Clinical review and updating are essential before practice use. The 2024 AAP opioid guideline is specific to acute outpatient settings; do not generalize its statements beyond their scope. AAPD document states revised 2022; check for subsequent updates.

No diagnosis, patient volume, application eligibility or guaranteed exam outcome is fabricated or inferred. BCH reports an average annual intake, but this curriculum does not use that as a current quota or case-volume claim.

unknownDurationItems.reason: Accessible duration not structurally supported by evidence.

topicGaps: 33.7336 hours remain below the 36-hour target floor after counting six unique publicly listed recordings totaling 8159 seconds (2.2664 hours). The EMSC duration pages report five runtimes at whole-minute precision; only the 8:59 SKIP video has a second-level runtime. No scripted or planned minutes are included.

Recorded-video coverage is still sparse: six additions focus on emergency pain, sickle-cell acute/chronic pain, psychological strategies, an intranasal demonstration, comfort positioning, and needle fear. Insufficient verified lecture coverage remains for pediatric pain neuroscience/development, validated assessment across neonatal and disability contexts, perioperative/regional anesthesia, medication pharmacology/adjuvant safety, cancer and palliative pain, headache/orofacial, visceral/abdominal, neuropathic and musculoskeletal syndromes, CRPS evaluation, research methods and interventional/procedural pain.

The 43-minute OPENPediatrics forum provides cognitive coverage of pediatric chronic and procedural pain psychology but is not a substitute for full rehabilitation training; the 46-minute sickle-cell talk and 28-minute ED overview are historical expert education, not current protocols. Apply date- and setting-specific guidelines and current institutional pathways.

The original UCSF pediatric pain lecture remains a useful public candidate but exact full runtime was not verified, so it remains in unknownDurationItems and is not counted. ChildKind archive recordings have relevant content but no individual duration ledger. OPENPediatrics advertises approximately three hours for an entire course without a per-recording measured ledger. Mary Bridge requires paid registration; Nemours source expiry remains unresolved.

The free public EMSC/HRSA-supported resource index gives exact minute-level duration labels and embeds the counted watch pages. Whole-minute entries are conservatively represented as the stated number of minutes in seconds, with 60-second precision recorded; EMSC does not expose second-level player runtimes. End-to-end playback was not tested using a stateful browser.

Topic gaps remain in pediatric-specialty depth; the ABA Pain Medicine blueprint is an adult/interdisciplinary parent-specialty blueprint, not a pediatric board exam or proof of pediatric readiness. No separate pediatric pain board examination was identified in the official materials already cited.

Five full authored teaching episodes in the separate authored JSON are scripts only: none is recorded, rendered, uploaded, or included in verifiedExternalHours. Their teaching cannot close the media-hour gap.

practiceQuestions.stem: A verbally communicative 10-year-old is asked to rate acute pain. Which approach best follows pediatric pain-assessment guidance?

options.text: Use self-report when developmentally able, select a validated scale consistently, and reassess after intervention.
Use the caregiver’s estimate in place of the child’s report.
Use heart rate as the primary pain score.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Self-report is preferred when possible; the same developmentally appropriate tool should be used and pain reassessed. Vital signs are not a substitute for report.

practiceQuestions.stem: A preverbal infant is undergoing a painful procedure. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: No change in heart rate establishes absence of pain.
Use an age-appropriate behavioral measure alongside clinical context; absence of physiologic change does not rule out pain.
Caregiver input should never be considered.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Behavioral scales and caregiver input may help when self-report is not possible; physiologic signs alone are unreliable and their absence does not exclude pain.

practiceQuestions.stem: In the 2024 AAP outpatient guideline, the recommended overall strategy for acute pain is:

options.text: Opioid monotherapy whenever pain is severe.
Multimodal care using appropriate nonpharmacologic, nonopioid and, when needed, opioid therapies.
Avoid all opioids in every pediatric acute pain circumstance.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAP KAS 1 recommends multimodal treatment; KAS 2 says not to prescribe opioids as monotherapy. Opioids remain an option when indicated.

practiceQuestions.stem: Under the AAP 2024 acute outpatient guideline, which codeine/tramadol statement is correct?

options.text: Do not prescribe codeine or tramadol for acute pain in children younger than 12 years.
They are preferred first line after tonsillectomy.
They are unrestricted in adolescents with obstructive sleep apnea.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAP KAS 4.1 prohibits codeine/tramadol in children <12; separate restrictions apply after tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy under 18 and to adolescents with obesity, OSA or severe lung disease.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with persistent pain has missed school and stopped sports although pain intensity varies. A useful chronic-pain assessment should additionally prioritize:

options.text: Function, sleep, school, social participation and psychosocial context.
A one-time numeric score only.
Repeated imaging until a structural cause is found.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Chronic pain assessment includes the impact on daily functioning and psychosocial context; no single intensity score captures disability or progress.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which broad approach best aligns with WHO guidance for chronic pain in children?

options.text: Use a physical, psychological and pharmacological framework tailored to the child and context.
Use opioids as first-line for primary chronic pain.
Treat physical function as irrelevant until pain is zero.

practiceQuestions.rationale: WHO guideline addresses physical, psychological and pharmacological interventions. It does not imply one universal treatment or promise pain elimination.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has disproportionate persistent limb pain, allodynia and color/temperature changes after a minor injury. Which is the most appropriate educational framing?

options.text: CRPS is possible, but consider differential diagnoses; clinical diagnosis rests on history/exam and multidisciplinary rehabilitation is central.
A normal imaging study alone proves CRPS.
The only appropriate treatment is a procedure.

practiceQuestions.rationale: BCH notes clinical diagnosis and selective tests to exclude other causes; multimodal care including PT and psychological support is emphasized.

practiceQuestions.stem: When planning prevention for an elective needle procedure, which package is most consistent with IASP pediatric guidance?

options.text: Age-appropriate topical anesthesia, infant breastfeeding/sucrose when appropriate, comfort positioning and distraction.
Routine restraint and reassurance that it will not hurt.
Analgesia only after the procedure.

practiceQuestions.rationale: IASP describes a bundle including topical anesthesia, feeding/sucrose for infants, comfort positioning and distraction, with respectful neutral language.
practiceQuestions.domain: Clinical States—Acute Pain, Pain due to Trauma, and Procedural Pain

practiceQuestions.stem: The 2025 ACGME Pain Medicine requirements specify a program length of:

options.text: 12 months.
3 months.
24 months.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME 4.1 requires 12 months; BCH separately describes its optional non-ACGME pathway as individualized 3–12 months.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately describes the ABA Pain Medicine exam blueprint?

options.text: It is a 200-item cognitive examination divided into General and Clinical States at 50% each.
It is a pediatric-only examination with guaranteed passing after a 36-hour course.
It certifies procedure competence through video viewing.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The published ABA blueprint specifies 200 single-best-answer questions with General and Clinical States each 50%; it does not establish pediatric-only certification or predict passage/procedural skill.

unitMap.text: Perinatal pathology: maternal–placental–fetal relationships
coveredTopics: Placental grossing, Amsterdam patterns, maternal vascular malperfusion, fetal vascular malperfusion, acute/chronic inflammation, twin placentation

Placental specimen orientation and adequacy; structured description before lesion labels; placental tumors and implantation disorders; maternal versus fetal vascular lesion patterns; twin placentation and lesion attribution (ABPath specification §1).

unitMap.text: Fetal/neonatal pathophysiology and perinatal autopsy
coveredTopics: Fetal growth/development, stillbirth, neonatal adaptation, iatrogenic injury, autopsy and clinicopathologic correlation
Fetal demise and postmortem change; growth/maturation, hydrops, congenital infection, prematurity complications and limits of causal/timing inference (ABPath specification §2).

unitMap.text: Developmental pathology, syndromes, and congenital anomalies
coveredTopics: Malformation complexes, dysmorphology, metabolic/genetic disorders, fetal specimens, pattern recognition

Developmental anatomy; malformation versus deformation, disruption, sequence and association; chromosomal and metabolic differentials; when to recommend genetics/ancillary testing without asserting a syndrome (ABPath specification §§1–3).

unitMap.text: Pediatric neoplasia, ancillary testing, and diagnostic integration
coveredTopics: Neuroblastic tumors, Wilms tumor, Ewing family, rhabdomyosarcoma, germ-cell tumors, retinoblastoma, hepatoblastoma, soft tissue and CNS tumors

Morphology-first differential for pediatric neoplasia; age/site context; sample triage; immunohistochemistry, flow, cytogenetics and molecular test selection; distinguish classification, prognostic factors and clinical risk assignment (ABPath §§3, 13, 20).

unitMap.text: Cardiovascular, respiratory, mediastinal, and special senses
coveredTopics: Congenital heart pathology, sudden death patterns, neonatal lung, cystic lesions, mediastinal tumors, eye/ear pathology

Congenital cardiac anatomy and developmental lesions; neonatal lung maturity and prematurity-associated injury; mediastinal lesions; eye and ear developmental pathology; sampling and age-aware differentials (ABPath §§4, 5, 8).

unitMap.text: Central and peripheral nervous system
coveredTopics: Embryology, neonatal brain injury, pediatric CNS tumors, malformations, peripheral nerve
Developmental malformations, hypoxic-ischemic and hemorrhagic injury, infection and tumors; topographic localization, age, clinical timeline and limits of postmortem attribution (ABPath §§2, 6, 22).

unitMap.text: Skin, soft tissue, and musculoskeletal pathology
coveredTopics: Congenital lesions, vascular anomalies, small round cell tumors, skeletal lesions, Ewing-family diagnostic approach
Age/site-driven classification of pediatric cutaneous and soft-tissue lesions; vascular anomalies; skeletal development and tumors; ancillary testing and specimen constraints (ABPath §§7, 18, 19).

unitMap.text: Gastrointestinal tract and Hirschsprung disease
coveredTopics: Hirschsprung disease, NEC, congenital enteropathies, inflammatory bowel disease, GI tumors, pediatric GI surgical specimens

Biopsy orientation and mucosal/submucosal adequacy; Hirschsprung disease; necrotizing enterocolitis; congenital enteropathies; inflammatory and infectious mimics; pediatric GI tumor patterns (ABPath §9).

unitMap.text: Hepatobiliary and pancreatic pathology
coveredTopics: Neonatal cholestasis, biliary atresia, metabolic liver disease, pediatric liver tumors, pancreas

Age-based cholestasis differential; biliary atresia and mimics; metabolic/infectious disease; hepatoblastoma and other liver tumors; clinicopathologic correlation without substituting morphology for clinical testing (ABPath §10).

unitMap.text: Renal, urinary, endocrine, and reproductive pathology
coveredTopics: Wilms/other renal tumors, nephrogenic rests, congenital nephropathies, endocrine lesions, gonadal/gynecologic pathology

Congenital renal anomalies, pediatric renal tumors, nephrogenic rests, endocrine disorders, gonadal development and disorders of sexual development; treatment-context-aware synoptic reporting (ABPath §§11, 12, 15–17).

unitMap.text: Hematolymphoid, immunopathology, and pediatric laboratory medicine
coveredTopics: Leukemia/lymphoma, immune disorders, transfusion, clinical chemistry, microbiology, cytology

Age-aware leukemia/lymphoma and immune disorder workup; morphology integrated with flow/IHC/genomics; transfusion, hematology, microbiology and clinical chemistry interfaces; test validation and limits (ABPath §§13, 20).

unitMap.text: Quality, communication, forensic context, and professional practice
coveredTopics: Quality systems, laboratory management, documentation, consent, child death investigation, consultation and multidisciplinary communication

Autopsy consent/documentation and forensic context; urgent communication and consultation; laboratory quality systems, management, specimen tracking, ethics and boundaries of educational self-study (ABPath §§20–22).

topicGaps: Verified recordings still concentrate on placenta/perinatal topics, neonatal cholestasis, Hirschsprung disease, and extended Ewing-family tumors. One additional free ARUP placental lecture adds 0.8139 h; it does not broaden the verified organ-system video base.

No counted full-length recording established for most board domains: developmental/genetic syndromes, cardiovascular, respiratory/mediastinal, CNS, skin/special senses, renal/endocrine/reproductive, hematolymphoid/laboratory medicine, autopsy/forensic and laboratory quality/management. Topic lists and authored scripts are not rendered video.

Original teaching inputs below add source-grounded instruction in selected high-yield gaps but do not supply the remaining 20.1719 h of verified video. Other listed organ-system gaps need clinician-authored and reviewed teaching, especially where primary source detail and publicly reusable images are unavailable.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Pathology (ABPath), Pediatric Pathology subspecialty certification examination
medical.boardStatus: A distinct ABPath Pediatric Pathology subspecialty certification exam exists. Official description lists a one-day computer-based exam with 170 written/practical questions (3 h 8 min) and 65 virtual microscopy questions (3 h 15 min); all one-best-answer.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: A course does not create eligibility. ABPath states subspecialty candidates need current primary or subspecialty certification from ABPath or another ABMS board and must meet current training, licensure and other application rules; the exact case/education pathway must be checked directly with ABPath. Boston Children’s states applicants generally need AP board certification/eligibility, with exceptional candidates sometimes entering after two AP years; that is a programme admission statement, not a guarantee of ABPath exam eligibility. Verify current requirements with ABPath and the program. No certification/pass outcome is promised.

officialProgrammes.institution: Boston Children’s Hospital (Harvard Medical School teaching hospital affiliate)
officialProgrammes.name: Pediatric Pathology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page calls this a one-year ACGME-approved program. Describes pediatric surgical pathology and autopsy; pulmonary, neuropathology, dermatopathology, GI, congenital cardiac, renal, electron microscopy, hematopathology, immunopathology, cytogenetics and molecular diagnostics; Brigham and Women’s perinatal/placental rotations; curriculum summary emphasizes pediatric surgical pathology, GI, autopsy, perinatal/placental, pediatric neuropathology and hematopathology, with elective and scholarly time. Public page is a program summary, not the full fellow syllabus or a public lecture schedule.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Packet lists one actual clinical physician fellowship at Boston Children’s Hospital. This is not a residency, combined program or generic fellowship directory label. No separate Harvard Medical School institutional fellowship variant or Johns Hopkins pediatric pathology track was verified from this packet/research; the official program is Boston Children’s. The two-year focus/research option mentioned on the official page is an optional extension of that fellowship, not a separate board or combined specialty. PathElective and SPP resources are educational supplements, not additional institutional clinical programs. No non-physician/research-only track included.
sourceCaveats: Boston Children’s official page directly confirms program type, one-year length and selected curriculum; it does not publish a complete syllabus, program-wide case counts, or full didactic video archive.
ACGME requirements effective 2026 include training/case expectations for accredited programs; they are not evidence of any individual fellow’s actual case volume or a self-study requirement.
ABPath public content specifications are a blueprint guide, not an exhaustive exam-content promise or course endorsement. Current eligibility rules can change and must be verified directly.
Current free lecture evidence is only 15.014 hours. This does not satisfy the 36-hour requested floor. No generated/planned video counts as completed or ready.
Public viewing of a clinical image or lecture does not grant a right to copy, host, remix, or redistribute. Links are provided without rehosting.

Human clinical review is not performed. Do not use this curriculum for individual patient diagnosis or treatment. Independent education grants no affiliation, accredited training, licensure, board eligibility, procedure competence, or certification.

No counted full-length recording established for most board domains: developmental/genetic syndromes, cardiovascular, respiratory/mediastinal, CNS, skin/special senses, renal/endocrine/reproductive, hematolymphoid/laboratory medicine, autopsy/forensic and laboratory quality/management. practiceQuestions.stem: Which framework distinguishes maternal vascular malperfusion from fetal vascular malperfusion in a placental report?

options.text: Amsterdam Placental Workshop Group consensus terminology
FIGO ovarian staging
PI-RADS
COG renal stage

practiceQuestions.rationale: The Amsterdam consensus standardizes lesion sampling/definitions and major patterns including MVM and FVM; terminology requires correlation and is not proof of causation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A trainee sees a placental lesion associated with fetal growth restriction. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.text: The lesion alone proves the cause of growth restriction
Record the lesion using accepted criteria and integrate clinical context; avoid inferring causality from association alone
A single lesion always establishes timing
Do not report placental findings

practiceQuestions.rationale: Morphologic placental patterns may associate with adverse outcomes, but clinicopathologic correlation is needed; avoid deterministic causal claims.

practiceQuestions.stem: For neuroblastoma, which histologic features are explicitly central to INPC assessment?

options.text: Schwannian stroma, differentiation, and mitosis-karyorrhexis index
PI-RADS score and Gleason grade
Tumor necrosis alone
Ki-67 alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI PDQ describes stroma, neuroblastic maturation and MKI as INPC parameters; age also influences favorable/unfavorable grouping.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about pediatric renal tumor staging is correct when using the CAP Wilms protocol?

options.text: COG and SIOP stages are interchangeable regardless of pretreatment
Select staging framework appropriate to treatment protocol; COG and SIOP criteria differ
Assign both without knowing clinical treatment
Stage is determined solely by tumor size

practiceQuestions.rationale: CAP directs completion of COG or SIOP staging based on the treatment protocol; preoperative therapy changes the interpretation framework.

practiceQuestions.stem: A suspected Hirschsprung disease biopsy lacks the expected submucosal compartment. Best next interpretive step?

options.text: Issue definitive absence-of-ganglion diagnosis from this specimen
Document sampling limitation and seek adequate, appropriately oriented tissue with ancillary testing as indicated
Use placental scoring
Report only clinical diagnosis

practiceQuestions.rationale: Adequacy and tissue level matter in evaluating aganglionosis; pathology should not overstate when required diagnostic compartments are absent.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which best describes ABPath pediatric pathology exam format on the official description page?

options.text: Only oral examination
Computer-based written/practical and virtual microscopy sections
Glass-slide practical only
No images

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official description specifies a one-day computer-based exam with combined written/practical and virtual microscopy sections.

practiceQuestions.stem: What does the ACGME standard specify for pediatric pathology fellowship length?

options.text: Six months
12 months
24 months universally
No duration

practiceQuestions.rationale: The currently linked ACGME Pediatric Pathology requirements state a 12-month program; the official Boston Children’s page also describes a one-year program.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the public SPP neuroblastoma atlas?

options.text: Its image license is explicitly CC BY
SPP describes annotated atlas as based on central review files; use link-only absent explicit reuse license
It is a synthetic dataset
It is a board exam bank

practiceQuestions.rationale: SPP practice resources identify the neuroblastoma atlas and provenance but no permissive re-use license; free access does not itself grant copying rights.

practiceQuestions.stem: A congenital infection diagnosis is being considered. Which resource is authoritative for current clinical management context but not a stand-alone tissue-diagnosis rule?

options.text: CDC Congenital Syphilis STI Treatment Guidelines
CAP Wilms protocol
ABPath exam blueprint
SPP atlas

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC guidelines provide infection clinical/testing guidance; they do not replace tissue-based differential or local diagnostic protocols.

practiceQuestions.stem: ABPath subspecialty candidate status should be represented how in this course?

options.text: Any course completer is board eligible
Certification eligibility depends on current ABPath rules including primary/subspecialty certification and training/licensure; check board directly
Boston Children’s affiliation confers exam access
Passing this course grants certification

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPath publishes specific requirements for education, licensure and training. An independent course creates no eligibility or credential.

unitMap.text: Developmental respiratory physiology, airway mechanics and symptom framing
Pulmonary function testing and diagnostic reasoning
Neonatal and infant lung disease
Airway and lung malformations; acute infections
Asthma: diagnosis, control, severe disease and therapeutics
Cystic fibrosis and CFTR-related disorders
Bronchiectasis and chronic suppurative lung disease
Respiratory failure, pulmonary vascular disease and critical illness
Sleep-disordered breathing and neuromuscular respiratory disease
Restrictive, interstitial and diffuse lung disease
Systemic, environmental, exposure-related and rare respiratory disorders
Scholarly practice, equity, longitudinal care and integrative synthesis

topicGaps: The target of 36 verified recorded hours is met by the unique-duration ledger; this is a media-hour threshold only, not proof of board readiness or clinical competence. Authored scripts remain unrendered and are not video hours.

Substantial depth gaps remain in developmental physiology, age-spanning PFT/diagnostic methods, longitudinal asthma therapeutics, contemporary CF care, environmental injuries and exposures, scholarly practice and health-equity methods. Recordings are topic-specific conference sessions, not a systematic full syllabus.

ATS pediatric symposium recordings materially strengthen coverage in severe asthma, congenital anomalies, immunodeficiency-associated respiratory disorders, pulmonary arterial hypertension, primary ciliary dyskinesia, CF, technology dependence, ILD, sleep, and infections. Several are older recordings; current guideline review remains necessary.

No institutional complete didactic recordings or rotation schedules are publicly documented in the consulted Johns Hopkins program page; exact program rotations and protected teaching remain unavailable.
The public Johns Hopkins programme overview remains distinct from ABP blueprint and ACGME requirements; no private institutional syllabus or unobserved teaching content has been inferred.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship; independent board-oriented self-study (not accredited training)
boardNames: American Board of Pediatrics (ABP) — Pediatric Pulmonology subspecialty certification examination
medical.boardStatus: This is an actual pediatric physician subspecialty fellowship, not a generic directory label or research-only position. Johns Hopkins’ official program page identifies a 3-year ACGME-accredited Pediatric Pulmonary Fellowship. ABP publishes a separate Pediatric Pulmonology subspecialty certifying examination and a 19-domain blueprint effective for exams on/after 2026-11-01. The Hopkins page says select PhD applicants may be considered for postdoctoral work; that supplement is not physician fellowship/board training. No combined program is listed in the packet or verified. Alternative AOBP-specific certification routes were outside this packet and were not independently assessed.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This self-study course conveys no ABP eligibility. ABP requires three years full-time fellowship in an ACGME/RCPSC-accredited Pediatric Pulmonology program, prior General Pediatrics certification maintained as applicable, unrestricted license, director verification, scholarly activity requirements and passing the subspecialty exam. Confirm latest rules directly with ABP; institutional PhD postdoctoral consideration is not physician certification eligibility.

The page states MD/MBBS/DO and completed ACGME-accredited Pediatrics residency for physician fellowship consideration; it also considers select PhD applicants for postdoctoral work, not equivalent physician training or board eligibility.

topicGaps: The target of 36 verified recorded hours is met by the unique-duration ledger; this is a media-hour threshold only, not proof of board readiness or clinical competence. Authored scripts remain unrendered and are not video hours.

Substantial depth gaps remain in developmental physiology, age-spanning PFT/diagnostic methods, longitudinal asthma therapeutics, contemporary CF care, environmental injuries and exposures, scholarly practice and health-equity methods. Recordings are topic-specific conference sessions, not a systematic full syllabus.

ATS pediatric symposium recordings materially strengthen coverage in severe asthma, congenital anomalies, immunodeficiency-associated respiratory disorders, pulmonary arterial hypertension, primary ciliary dyskinesia, CF, technology dependence, ILD, sleep, and infections. Several are older recordings; current guideline review remains necessary.

No institutional complete didactic recordings or rotation schedules are publicly documented in the consulted Johns Hopkins program page; exact program rotations and protected teaching remain unavailable.
The public Johns Hopkins programme overview remains distinct from ABP blueprint and ACGME requirements; no private institutional syllabus or unobserved teaching content has been inferred.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 7-month-old has persistent tachypnea, hypoxemia and diffuse interstitial opacities after common causes are excluded. What is the best next general approach?

options.text: Assume aspiration is proven and treat empirically
Refer for knowledgeable pediatric ILD evaluation and stage noninvasive then selected specialized testing by context
Proceed directly to surgical lung biopsy in every infant
Use a normal chest radiograph to exclude chILD

practiceQuestions.rationale: ATS guidance describes context-sensitive specialist evaluation; imaging, echocardiography, infant PFT, genetics, BAL or biopsy may be considered. No single test is universal.

practiceQuestions.stem: A school-aged child with episodic wheeze has normal spirometry when well. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: Asthma is excluded
A single normal test when asymptomatic may not establish or exclude variable airflow limitation; reassess objective evidence and alternatives
Diagnose severe asthma immediately
Start biologic treatment without checking technique or adherence

practiceQuestions.rationale: Asthma diagnosis integrates variable symptoms and objective evidence where feasible, with reassessment and mimic/comorbidity evaluation. Follow current GINA; a well-state normal test does not alone rule out disease.

practiceQuestions.stem: A positive CF newborn screen with inconclusive initial results should be handled how?

options.text: Screen alone is diagnostic
Complete guideline-based diagnostic evaluation including sweat testing, genetic/clinical context, and appropriate specialist follow-up
Defer all evaluation until symptoms develop
Interpret one CFTR variant as definite CF without context

practiceQuestions.rationale: CFF diagnosis resources describe a multistep evaluation; positive screen is not itself a confirmed diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: For a child with CF, which statement about a public CF guideline is most defensible?

options.text: One old recommendation applies unchanged to all ages and all modulators
Use current age- and topic-specific guidance, verify evidence/date and individualized specialist context
Stop pulmonary care if symptoms improve
A class lecture replaces CF-center supervision

practiceQuestions.rationale: CFF organizes current topic and age-specific recommendations; treatment updates and patient factors matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: An infant with diffuse lung disease has an unremarkable initial basic evaluation and persistent symptoms. What genetic testing is specifically recommended by the cited ATS infancy guideline in that context?

options.text: Universal broad panel before any evaluation
Consider SFTPC and ABCA3 mutation testing if initial studies do not provide a diagnosis
Only CFTR sequencing is relevant
No genetic testing is appropriate in infancy

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ATS guideline recommends testing for SFTPC and ABCA3 mutations in infants beyond neonatal period with chILD syndrome when initial studies do not provide diagnosis; this is not an automatic universal test.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child snores nightly with witnessed pauses. Which diagnostic test is guideline-supported for suspected pediatric obstructive sleep apnea?

options.text: Home audio alone
Attended overnight polysomnography when clinically indicated
Adult home sleep apnea test as universal first-line test
Chest radiograph

practiceQuestions.rationale: AASM pediatric respiratory indications support polysomnography; testing decisions remain clinical and local.
practiceQuestions.domain: 9 Sleep-Disordered Breathing and Control of Breathing Disorders

practiceQuestions.stem: A school-aged child has persistent wet cough and recurrent infections with CT-confirmed bronchiectasis. What is the best reasoning frame?

options.text: Assume CF irrespective of tests
Investigate underlying causes and pair long-term plan with pediatric bronchiectasis guidance and airway clearance goals
Use bronchodilator alone as definitive therapy
Ignore microbiology because imaging is sufficient

practiceQuestions.rationale: Bronchiectasis has multiple etiologies; guidelines emphasize cause evaluation and longitudinal goals, not a single diagnosis or intervention.

practiceQuestions.stem: An infant with BPD is being considered for long-term respiratory support. Which principle is most appropriate?

options.text: Video-based self-study authorizes ventilator changes
Use multidisciplinary, supervised individualized assessment and longitudinal monitoring; do not infer a patient-specific weaning plan from a lecture
All preterm infants require identical support
A research webinar proves treatment efficacy

practiceQuestions.rationale: Clinical decisions require the child’s status and supervised specialist team. A conference recording is educational and cannot establish individualized management.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public pediatric CXR dataset is listed as de-identified. What does that permit for this course?

options.text: Unlimited reposting of downloaded images
Read the access license and conditions; link to dataset, do not copy/rehost or infer rare diagnoses from limited cases
Share dataset credentials freely
Treat labels as clinical gold standard

practiceQuestions.rationale: PediCXR states data were deidentified but requires acceptance of a credentialed license and restricts sharing; dataset has limitations and was designed for ML research.
practiceQuestions.domain: 18 Core Principles of Pulmonary Diagnosis and Monitoring Techniques

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner finds a recorded bronchoscopy demonstration online. Which boundary applies?

options.text: Viewing grants procedural competence
The recording may illustrate concepts but does not replace credentialed, supervised hands-on training and institutional authorization
Can perform bronchoscopy unsupervised after quiz
Any video can be redistributed freely
